chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from al-Husayn ibn 'Uthman, from سماعة ibn Mihran, from Abi Basir, who said:

I said to Abi 'Abdillah عليه السلام: We travel, and sometimes we are tried with a rain pool that is beside the village; there is feces in it, a boy urinates in it, and a beast urinates and defecates in it.
So he said: “If something concerning it arises in your heart, then do like this” — meaning, move the water apart with your hand — “then perform wudu (ablution), for the religion is not restrictive.
For Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: “He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship.”

key_terms.ٱفْرِجِ: separate or move aside, here referring to parting the water by hand
key_terms.ٱلدِّينَ: the religion, meaning the divinely legislated way
key_terms.ٱلْعَذِرَةُ: feces or filth present in the water
key_terms.ٱلْغَدِيرِ: a pool of collected water, here formed by rain

ai.seo_question: Can one perform wudu (ablution) from a rain pool near a village if it may contain impurities?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses ritual purity and the permissibility of using water from a rain pool that may be suspected of contamination. Imam al-Sadiq عليه السلام teaches that mere misgiving does not make the water unusable, and he supports this legal ease by citing the Quranic principle that Allah has not placed hardship in religion.
